name: Sh
title: Sh (POSIX.1-2024)

type.text: **All values are strings, and numbers live in a second grammar**: `x=1` and `x=abc` are the same assignment, and `$(( ... ))` evaluates a signed-integer expression that is re-parsed at each use
**No arrays and no associative arrays**: A list is a string split on `IFS`, and the specification provides no indexed or keyed aggregate
**No generics and no dispatch by type**: A routine is specialised only by its positional parameters, and behaviour is selected by the command name (T5, T9)
**One flat namespace**: The specification gives a function no local scope, so a function's working variables are the caller's variables (T6, T11)
**An unset name and an empty name are indistinguishable**: `set -u` turns a reference to an unset name into an error, but it is off by default and an empty value still passes
**Default and alternate expansions are part of the language**: `${var:-default}` and `${var:+alternate}` carry the missing-value case in the expansion itself, so many ad-hoc checks disappear

construction.text: **Global by default and mutable by default**: An assignment writes the single namespace, and only `readonly` fixes a value (C1, C2)
**No constructor or validation at the point of assignment**: Nothing checks a value when it is bound, so validation is written as a separate `case` statement or `test`

**Functions share the caller's variables**: The standard provides no local declaration — `local` is a ksh and Bash extension, and shells that offer it differ in detail — so a helper must save and restore every name it touches, or run in a subshell
**A subshell is a scope**: `( ... )` runs in a child process, so a subroutine is isolated from the parent's values by wrapping it
**Positional parameters are the argument list**: A function or a `sh -c` string reads its inputs as `$1`, `$2`, and so on, so a routine consumes its arguments instead of reading a global
**`ENV` separates interactive setup from scripts**: An interactive shell reads its personalisation file from `$ENV`, so a non-interactive script starts with none of it

memory.text: **No allocation or free in the language**: There is no pointer and no deallocation builtin; the shell owns every string
**A subshell releases its memory at exit**: `( ... )` ends and its environment is discarded, so temporary state does not survive it
**`unset` drops a name**: The shell reclaims the storage, so no free order and no double free can arise
**Assignment copies the value**: `b=$a` duplicates the string, and there is no way to reference a value without copying it
**A pipeline is a set of processes**: The shell forks each stage, so the memory cost of a pipeline is the sum of its parts
**Command substitution is buffered whole**: `$(cmd)` collects the entire output before the enclosing command runs, so the whole result is held in memory and then split

error.text: **No structured error path**: The entire apparatus is `$?` and `trap`, with no exception and no error value
**`$?` is lost by the next command**: Any command resets it, so an interposed test discards the failure
**Errors do not compose**: A failure is an exit status, so it cannot carry a payload, be returned as data, or be combined with another
**`set -e` is not a reliable policy**: `errexit` does not fire in `&&` and `||` chains, in conditions, or after a negation, so a wrapper that suppresses it changes the behaviour of the whole script
**There is no `ERR` trap in the standard**: Reporting and cleanup must be attached to `EXIT`, to a named signal, or to an explicit check after each command
**`trap ... EXIT` runs on every exit path**: Cleanup can be attached once and will run on a normal exit or on a handled signal

concurrency.text: **No concurrency primitives**: No lock, channel, semaphore, or await exists; the only parallel construct is `&`
**Pipelines are a first-class composition**: The pipeline is a core operator of the language, so stages are connected without the script manipulating file descriptors
**`wait` and `$!` make a job addressable**: `cmd &` records the process id in `$!`, so a script can wait for one job rather than for all of them
**A subshell isolates concurrent state**: `( ... ) &` gives a job its own copy of the environment, so the job cannot change the parent's values
**Background jobs share files and the working directory**: A `&` job inherits the environment, the umask, and the current directory, so ordering is unspecified unless the script waits
**No value comes back from a job**: A status arrives through `wait`, and a result must travel through a file, a pipe, or a named pipe

platform.text: **`sh` is an implementable name, not an implementation**: POSIX defines the language but not which program provides it, so `/bin/sh` is dash, ash, bash in POSIX mode, or a vendor shell depending on the system, and only the standard subset is portable
**POSIX guarantees that a shell exists**: Every conforming system provides `sh`, so a script invokes an interpreter without installing anything
**The standard is written for maximum reach**: The language contains no optional syntax that a conforming shell may omit
**Implementations are not equally complete**: An older `sh` may lack behaviour added in Issue 8, so a script that uses `pipefail` or `$'...'` is portable only to newer systems
**`sh -c` is the universal entry point**: `system()`, `make`, containers, and `cron` all use it, which makes the shell the assumed execution layer even when no script is written
**Extensions are common and not portable**: `local`, `[[ ... ]]`, arrays, and `function` are available in many `sh` implementations but are outside the standard

performance.text: **Interpreted with no compilation**: Each command is parsed and executed as text, and there is no artifact and no JIT
**A minimal implementation starts fast**: `dash` and `ash` reach the first command in a fraction of the time a feature-rich shell needs, which matters for the many `sh -c` calls in a build or a boot
**Builtins replace processes for common work**: `printf`, `read`, `test`, `getopts`, and parameter expansion avoid an external command
**Every external command forks**: The builtin set is small, so a loop that calls `sed`, `grep`, or `basename` per item pays a process per iteration
**Command substitution is buffered and re-split**: `$(cmd)` reads the whole output and then splits it on `IFS`, so a large result is walked twice
**Scripts pay no start-up configuration**: The `ENV` file is read only by an interactive shell, so a non-interactive script pays nothing for user setup

ecosystem.text: **No package manager**: There is no dependency mechanism for shell code, so shared routines are sourced from a directory or vendored
**Every UNIX-like system has an implementation**: Dash, ash and BusyBox `ash`, FreeBSD `sh`, ksh, and bash in POSIX mode all provide an `sh` mode, so a script always has a host
**The standard is published and maintained**: The Open Group Base Specifications define the language in one stable document with a change history
**Analysers target `sh` by default**: ShellCheck and similar tools treat `sh` as the base case, so a minimal script is the best-supported one
**`checkbashisms` detects non-portable constructs**: A script can be checked against the POSIX surface before it is released
**Most published shell libraries assume Bash**: They use arrays and `[[ ... ]]`, so they cannot be used in a strictly conforming script

evolution.text: **The standard moves slowly**: Issue 7 appeared in 2018 and Issue 8 in 2024, so a needed feature waits years for the committee
**The standard is backward compatible**: Issue 8 adds features and removes only what was already marked obsolescent, so old scripts keep running
**Removals are signposted for years**: `test`'s `-a` and `-o` primaries were marked obsolescent in Issue 7 before Issue 8 removed them
**The change history ships with the text**: Every change from the previous issue is recorded in the specification rationale
**Adoption lags publication**: A shipped `sh` may implement an older issue for years, so a script written to Issue 8 may not run on the host it is deployed to
**The committee decides on defect reports**: A change enters the standard only through an accepted interpretation, so the process is deliberate rather than responsive

domain.text: **Excellent fit for its intended domain**: Boot scripts, installers, container entrypoints, and `configure` scripts need the one interpreter that is always present
**Stop-gap automation is a native use**: A two-line `sh -c` avoids a build step and a binary, which is why build tools, `cron`, and orchestrators embed it
**Portable text filtering composes well**: Pipelines over `grep`, `sed`, and `awk` are the idiom the language was designed around
**Configuration and environment setup read cleanly**: Exporting variables, setting `umask`, and changing directories is a few lines
**Data structures push the script elsewhere**: Without arrays, a keyed or indexed collection becomes a temporary file and a series of `awk` invocations
**Not a general-purpose language**: The model is a shell over external commands, so a program with real logic belongs in another language

learning.text: **A small surface to learn**: Assignments, `if`, `case`, and pipelines cover most scripts, and the standard is short compared with `bash` or `zsh`
**Skills transfer upward**: Everything learned in `sh` applies to Bash, ksh, and zsh, which is why it is the usual starting point
**The specification is the reference**: A precise description of every construct exists in one place
**Quoting and word splitting trap newcomers**: `$var` unquoted splits and globs, so a space or an asterisk in a value changes the command
**`[` is a command, not syntax**: `test` parses its arguments, so an unquoted empty variable changes the argument count and can turn a test into an error or a truth
**The specification is written for implementers**: It is precise about behaviour and thin on explanation, so learners need other material

syntax.text: **The language is small and predictable**: Assignments, `if`, `while`, `for`, `case`, and pipelines cover the whole grammar
**Here-documents handle multi-line input**: `<<` and `<<-` embed a block of text in a script without escaping
**Expansion has five forms to remember**: `%`, `%%`, `#`, `##`, and `${#var}` are compact but each has its own rule
**Quoting rules are context-dependent**: Single quotes, double quotes, and backslash escapes each treat `$`, backtick, and newline differently
**`[` and `test` need the operands spaced out**: The bracket form requires a space after `[` and before `]`, which is easy to forget
**No `[[ ... ]]` in the standard**: The construct was removed from the shell language description in an early POSIX proposal, so richer tests are written with `case` or with `expr`

testing.text: **No test framework in the language**: A test is a script that checks `$?`, with no assertion, fixture, or reporting facility
**Faults appear only on the branch that runs**: With no static check, a mistyped variable or a missing file is found during the run
**A syntax check runs without execution**: `sh -n` parses a script and reports errors without running it
**`set -x` shows the expansion**: The traced command reveals how a value was split and quoted before it ran
**Exit status is a reliable oracle**: `$?` after a command gives one unambiguous value to assert on
**A test can be isolated with a subshell**: `( ... )` gives each case a fresh copy of the environment, so one case cannot leak into the next

security.text: **Command construction from text is the classic injection path**: A value expanded into a command line or passed to `eval` becomes code, so unquoted expansion of untrusted input is unsafe
**Weak typing removes a check the shell cannot make**: A value that should be a number, a path, or a flag is a string, and only the command that receives it can object
**`test` can be made argument-safe**: `[ "X$response" = "Xexpected" ]` or `${var:+...}` expansion removes the ambiguity that an unquoted variable introduces
**`set -f` disables globbing**: `noglob` stops an expanded `*` from becoming a path list
**`umask` is part of the language**: File-creation permissions are set inside the script rather than left to the ambient environment
**No memory-safety surface**: Strings are interpreter-managed, so a script has no buffer to overflow

tradeoffs: **Minimalism is the point**: The language is small because every construct must be implementable on every conforming system, so the absence of arrays is a scope decision
**Portability costs expressiveness**: Writing to the standard means doing without associative arrays, pattern-replacement expansions, and floating point
**No interactive features is a deliberate omission**: Line editing, history, and completion are terminal concerns and are kept out of the standard
**`/bin/sh` is a policy choice on each system**: A distribution links it to dash, bash, or another shell, and that choice is not the language's
**Integer arithmetic is the standard's floor**: A script that needs floating point calls an external tool, which is a design boundary rather than a defect
**The specification is written for implementers**: Its precision makes it slow to read, and that is the price of one text that many shells obey
verdict: sh is the smallest language in the shell family, and its coupling profile is the family floor: every value is a string, one namespace holds every name, a function has no private scope, and an error is an exit status rather than a value. What it returns for that price is reach — one text that every conforming system implements, so a script runs wherever POSIX is present, and its standard is slow to change but never breaks what it already promised. The ecosystem score reflects that trade: the tooling and the specification are complete and stable, while the glacial standardisation cycle and the missing test and error apparatus remain real costs.

energy.text: Every operation starts a process: time, and therefore energy, is dominated by process startup.

ai-readiness.text: A large training corpus and strong code-generation results: models write this language well [@joel2025lowresource; @effibenchx2025].

safety.text: No certified or standards-qualified path for safety-critical systems.

delivery.note: The installed interpreter reads the source at run time; no compiled unit crosses a boundary
